Good morning. Our museum wants kiosks that recognise the style of a painting from a photo. We worked on five styles: Baroque, Cubism, Impressionism, Pop Art and Ukiyo-e. The kiosks have small CPUs, the team is small and the budget is limited. So the director asks one question: is a neural network worth it in production, or would a simpler classical model do the job?

TRANSITION: To answer it, we did not jump straight to a big model. So now, here is our path: six steps.

Step one: the data, and a fair test. Step two: a baseline, a classical model without any neural network. Step three: our own neural network, an MLP. Step four: a pretrained ResNet18. Step five: a much bigger model, CLIP. Step six: all of them, criterion by criterion. Each model must beat the baseline, and fit on a kiosk.

TRANSITION: So now, let's start with step one: the data, and how we made the test fair.

We took 1 500 paintings from WikiArt, 300 per style. We cut them into three piles: 1 061 to train, 219 to validate, that is, to choose our settings, and 220 to test, only once, at the end. One rule matters a lot: all the paintings of a known painter go to the same pile. With a random split, 23 of our 32 known painters would be in two piles, and a model could learn to recognise Monet instead of Impressionism. With our split: zero.

TRANSITION: Our data is ready and our test is fair. So now, step two: the baseline, the score every model must beat.

Our baseline uses no neural network. It cannot read raw pixels well, so we first describe each painting with 102 hand-made numbers: 82 for its colours, and 20 for the direction and strength of its brush strokes. Then a random forest: 500 decision trees. Each tree asks yes or no questions on these numbers, like "many dark colours?", until it names a style. They vote, and the vote cancels many mistakes. We chose its settings on validation: 63.5 percent. This is the score to beat.

TRANSITION: We saw that the baseline reaches 63.5 percent. So now, step three: can our own neural network beat it?

Our first neural network is the simplest one of the course: a multi-layer perceptron built from nn.Linear layers and ReLU. Before trusting it, we ran two checks. First, a model that knows nothing should have a loss of ln 5, about 1.61. Ours started at 1.99, too confident, so we made its last layer smaller and got 1.59. Second, it must be able to learn one small batch by heart: it does, 100 percent. The training accuracy goes to 99.7 percent, but the validation accuracy stays around 40 percent. This is overfitting: the network learns the paintings by heart.

TRANSITION: We saw that our MLP is overfitting. So now, we look inside its training and try to fix it.

Before fixing it, we looked inside the network: the gradient reaches every layer and only 4 percent of the neurons are dead. The training is healthy: the problem really is overfitting. Then we attacked it with the tools of session 6. Together, weight decay, dropout, batch norm, flips and early stopping take the MLP from 38.8 to 45.5 percent, and the gap from 0.61 to 0.12. But it stays far below the baseline: 45.5 against 63.5. It finds only 7 percent of the Cubist paintings: it sees colours, not shapes.

TRANSITION: Our MLP stays below the baseline. So now, step four: a model that sees shapes, and that is fast.

To see shapes, we need a network made for images: a convolutional network, or CNN. The brief asks for a ResNet, a family of CNNs that won the ImageNet competition in 2015. ResNet18 is its smallest member: light enough for a kiosk, and PyTorch gives it already trained. Its 18 layers slide small filters over the picture: the first layers find edges and colours, the next ones textures, the last ones shapes. "Res" means residual: shortcuts between its layers let a deep network learn well. ResNet18 already learned this on 1.2 million ImageNet photos, and we only have 1 061 paintings, so we never retrain all of it. It turns each painting into 512 numbers, and we replace its last layer by our own, for our 5 styles. We tried two ways. Frozen: only our new layer learns, 2 565 weights. Fine-tuned: the last block learns again too, 8.4 million weights. Like hiring an experienced art expert: frozen, we only teach them our five style names; fine-tuned, we also retrain their eye.

TRANSITION: We saw how ResNet18 works. So now, let's see what it gives on our paintings.

These are the final tests, run once at the very end: 440 paintings never seen before, our test pile and 220 new paintings from another part of WikiArt. The fine-tuned ResNet18 gets 87.8 percent: 22 points above the baseline, and twice our MLP. On validation, the frozen and the fine-tuned versions were too close to choose, on only 219 paintings. On the tests, the fine-tuned one wins by 5 points, and it is not luck. That is why we keep the fine-tuned one. And it does see shapes: on validation, the ResNet finds 71 percent of the Cubist paintings, against 7 for our MLP. We monitored it like the MLP: the gap between train and validation is only 0.09, against 0.61 for our first MLP.

TRANSITION: We saw that ResNet18 beats the baseline by far. So now, step five: would a much bigger model do even better?

ResNet18 is one of the smallest image networks, so we also tried one of the biggest: CLIP ViT-L/14, by OpenAI. A transformer, like BERT, that learned from 400 million Internet images and their captions. We used it like ResNet18: frozen, with our linear head. On validation, it reaches 96.3 percent: the best of all our models. But look at the price. One photo takes 4.6 seconds on one CPU thread, 38 times ResNet18, and its file weighs 1.2 gigabytes, 27 times more. On a kiosk, that is about 18 seconds per photo: too slow and too big. It would need a GPU. And it has probably seen WikiArt paintings during its training.

TRANSITION: We saw that CLIP is more accurate, but does not fit on a kiosk. So now, step six: all our models side by side, criterion by criterion.

On the same 440 new paintings, the baseline gets 65 percent, our MLP 42, the fine-tuned ResNet18 88, and CLIP 96. Then the kiosk criteria, fixed before the tests: one second per photo on the kiosk, and a file under 200 megabytes. ResNet18 answers in 121 milliseconds on our laptop, weighs 45 megabytes and retrains in 3.4 minutes. CLIP breaks both limits. ResNet18 is the only model that is both accurate and fits the kiosk. So our final choice is a fine-tuned ResNet18: it answers the director's question. Yes, a neural network is worth it. One visitor in eight gets a wrong style, against one in three with the baseline, and it runs on a modest kiosk. Before launch, we test it on real kiosk photos. Thank you. We are happy to take your questions.
